To make real hypotheses: se + present → present / future / imperative.
Not to put the conditional after "se": Se è…, NOT "Se sarebbe…".
To form the past conditional: avrei + participle, sarei + participle.
To express an unfulfilled wish: Avrei voluto…, Sarei venuto, ma…
To express a reproach: Avresti dovuto dirmelo!
To discuss an important subject as a family and reach a compromise.

Stress on "VREY" and "VRES": a-VREY, a-VRES-tee. Not "a-vrey-stee"!
When something is possible and real ("if it's a girl…"), Italian uses SE + PRESENT, and in the main clause the present, future or imperative:
If it's a girl, we'll call her Viola.
If it rains, we'll stay at home.
If you come, I'll make you dinner.
If you have time, call me!
NO conditional after "se": "Se è una bambina", NOT "Se sarebbe una bambina". Just like English: "if it is", not "if it would be" (for real hypotheses).
If the hypothesis is clearly about the future, you can put the future in BOTH parts (especially in writing). In speech, the present is just as correct:
If it's a boy, we'll call him Aldo.
If you come to Florence, I'll take you to the Uffizi.
If you come to Florence, I'll take you to the Uffizi.
Don't mix the future and present at random: "Se sarà…, lo chiameremo" or "Se è…, lo chiamiamo". Both are fine.
3. The past conditional: how to form it
It's formed with the auxiliary (avere / essere) in the present conditional + participle. Like English "would have wanted", "would have gone".
NOT "vorrei voluto" or "vorrei avuto". The auxiliary is always AVERE or ESSERE: "avrei voluto", "sarei venuto".
4. When to use the past conditional
I'd have liked an Italian name.
something you would have done, but didn't
I'd have come, but I was ill.
"Avrei dovuto" = I should have, "avresti dovuto" = you should have. In English "should have" is the same for every person; in Italian it's conjugated!
Past conditional (in the past, didn't happen)
The past conditional often shows regret: the thing never happened. You'll use it a lot in chapter 41, with "se avessi…, avrei…".

Se sarebbe un maschio, lo chiamiamo Aldo.
Se è un maschio, lo chiamerebbe Aldo.

Nobody had warned them that choosing a name was harder than restoring a Caravaggio. For the painting, at least, there were rules. For the name, on the other hand, there were two families, two languages, three grandmothers and a nine-year-old boy with a list of forty suggestions, including Batman, Ferrari and "Gelato".

Rosaria had phoned from Naples on the first of January, even before the new year greetings: "If it's a girl and you don't call her Assunta, Grandma will be hurt." Half an hour later Grandma Assunta herself had phoned: "If you name her after me, I'll cut you out of my will. Assunta is an old woman's name. I'd have liked to be called Sofia."

From Sibiu, Ion had been simpler: "If it's a boy, Ion. If it's a girl, Ioana. End of discussion." Doina, on the other hand, hadn't said anything. "If I give you a name, you'll feel obliged," she had explained. "And I don't want that. You'll choose. Whatever name it is will be the most beautiful name in the world." Matei had thought his mother was the wisest person in the family. And the craftiest.

At the workshop, Bellini had an opinion too. "If you call the baby Caravaggio, I'll fire you both," he had said without looking up from his painting. Then, after a long silence, he had added in a low voice: "My grandfather would have said that a name is like a signature on a painting. It doesn't have to be big. It has to be true."

For weeks Matei and Giulia argued, lovingly but passionately. He suggested Romanian names she couldn't pronounce. She suggested Neapolitan names he found too long. "You should have married a girl from Sibiu," Giulia would say. "And you could have married a Neapolitan," Matei would reply. "At least then we'd only have one kind of name to look for." Then they would laugh, and start all over again.

One Saturday in February they went to the Uffizi with Pietro, who had promised not to say "Batman" even once. They walked along the corridors, past the Madonnas, the saints, the goddesses. Every painting had a name: Lucrezia, Simonetta, Caterina, Flora. "If it's a girl, Flora?" Matei asked. "Flora Popa?" Giulia replied. "It sounds like a brand of margarine."

In the end they stopped in front of Botticelli's Primavera. Pietro sat on the floor to count the flowers in the meadow: after ten minutes he had reached a hundred and ninety. Giulia, meanwhile, was looking at a little violet flower near Flora's foot. "Look," she said. "A violet. They've been my favourite flowers since I was little. Grandma Assunta always put them on her sewing machine."

Then she turned to Matei. "If it's a girl… Viola?" Matei didn't answer. He was looking at the little flower, but he seemed to be seeing something else, very far away. "What is it?" Giulia asked. "My grandmother, my mother's mother," Matei said quietly. "She was called Viorica. In Romanian it means 'little violet'. She died when I was five. I only remember her hands, and a song."

Giulia took his hand. "She's the woman in the portrait with the blue veil, isn't she? The one with her eyes." Matei nodded. "My mother would have liked to call Ilinca that, but my father had already chosen. Grandma would have been happy. I'd have liked her to meet you." Pietro, on the floor, looked up: "Two hundred and twenty flowers! And Viola is a really beautiful name. More beautiful than Batman."

That evening they also decided on a name for a boy. It was Giulia who suggested it, and Matei said yes at once, without arguing, for the first time in two months: Aldo. Like Graziella's husband, the mud angel, the man with the red bicycle and the notches on the door. "If it's a boy, Aldo," said Matei. "If it's a girl, Viola. And if it's two…" "If it's two," said Giulia, "I'm running away to Iceland."

But they didn't tell anyone. "If we tell Graziella, tomorrow the whole of via Maggio will know," said Giulia. "If we tell my mother, the day after tomorrow the whole of Naples will know." "And if we tell Pietro…" Matei began. "Pietro already knows," said Giulia. "But Pietro has promised. And when Pietro promises, he's more reliable than a notary."

They wrote the two names on a sheet of paper, put it in an envelope and sealed it with the red wax Matei used for restoration documents. On the envelope Giulia wrote: "To be opened in May." Then they put it on the shelf above the bed, next to the two brushes, Ion's watch and Doina's blanket. The shelf was full by now. And there were still three months to go.
